card.chief_complaint: looks worse with hypotension after recent STEMI

ask.changes_what: Shaking chills should prompt blood cultures and a search for a bacteremic source (line, biliary, urinary, endovascular); no chills supports withholding cultures when pretest probability is low.
ask.do_not_use_when: The RCE conclusions do not apply to immunocompromised patients or when endocarditis is suspected; in those groups obtain cultures regardless of chills.
ask.escalation_warning: Rigors with hypotension, altered mentation or a central line indicate probable bacteremia/sepsis: cultures, source control and antibiotics within the hour.

evidence.citation: Coburn B, Morris AM, Tomlinson G, Detsky AS. Does this adult patient with suspected bacteremia require blood cultures? JAMA. 2012;308(5):502-511.
evidence.population: Adult immunocompetent patients in whom bacteremia was suspected (35 studies; 4566 bacteremia and 25,946 negative episodes)
evidence.quote: The severity of chills graded on an ordinal scale (shaking chills, LR, 4.7; 95% CI, 3.0-7.2) may be more useful.
evidence.reference_standard: Blood cultures
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia (true-positive blood culture)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: Shaking chills showed a specificity of 90.3% (95% CI 89.2-91.5) and positive likelihood ratio of 4.65 (95% CI 2.95-6.86).
evidence.reference_standard: Blood cultures
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: shaking chills (whole-body shaking under a thick blanket)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: The absence of chills showed a sensitivity of 87.5% (95% CI 74.4-94.5) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11-0.51).
evidence.reference_standard: Blood cultures
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: any chills (sensitivity and LR- refer to absence of chills)

ask.how: Ask the patient (or witnesses) whether they have had chills and grade the worst episode: mild = feeling cold, needing a jacket; moderate = needing a thick blanket; shaking chills = whole-body shaking even under a thick blanket. Record timing relative to fever and any line, procedure or infusion.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of any chills lowers the probability of bacteremia (LR- 0.24) but does not exclude it, particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients who may not mount rigors.
ask.pitfalls: Rigors also occur with malaria, transfusion or drug reactions, and after amphotericin or contaminated infusions; the grading relies on patient recall and the RCE data exclude immunocompromised patients and suspected endocarditis.
ask.positive_finding: Shaking (rigor-grade) chills raise the probability of bacteremia about 4.7-fold (LR+ 4.7, 95% CI 3.0-7.2; specificity 0.90) and justify blood cultures before antibiotics.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or witness able to describe the episode; ask before antipyretics blunt recall.
ask.title: Rigors / shaking chills

ask.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant volume loss - IV access, fluid/blood, search for bleeding source; negative: does not exclude moderate haemorrhage, use labs/other findings.
ask.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is already hypotensive, in shock, or with suspected unstable spine/pelvic injury.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing in patients who are hypotensive supine, obtunded, or at high fall risk; do not apply the volunteer-derived numbers uncritically to elderly patients on antihypertensives, beta-blockers or with autonomic neuropathy.
ask.escalation_warning: Inability to stand because of dizziness in a patient with suspected bleeding indicates large-volume loss: obtain large-bore access, type and crossmatch, and escalate immediately.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from LARGE acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness (preventing upright vitals) OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from MODERATE acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

ask.how: After supine vitals, stand the patient (with assistance) and ask about dizziness while measuring pulse and BP at about 1 minute. 'Severe' means dizziness so marked the patient cannot stay standing long enough for upright vitals or nearly faints; record it as a positive finding in its own right, together with any pulse increment of 30/min or more.
ask.negative_finding: Absence is reassuring only against large blood loss (sensitivity 0.97); after moderate (450-630 mL) loss the finding is usually absent (sensitivity 0.22), so a negative test does not exclude clinically important haemorrhage.
ask.pitfalls: Mild postural dizziness has no proven diagnostic value; supine tachycardia or hypotension is often absent even after 1 L loss. Evidence comes from healthy volunteers after phlebotomy, not from elderly or medicated ED patients, in whom baseline orthostatic symptoms are common.
ask.positive_finding: Severe postural dizziness (or a postural pulse increment >=30/min) is highly specific (0.98) for hypovolaemia from blood loss and is present in almost all subjects after large (630-1150 mL) blood loss.
ask.prerequisites: Supine rest for at least 2 minutes before standing; an assistant to prevent a fall. Sitting is not an adequate substitute for standing.
ask.title: Severe postural dizziness / inability to stand for vitals

ask.changes_what: Positive: escalate to ADD-RS assessment, CXR/D-dimer and CT angiography as appropriate; negative onset lowers but does not eliminate dissection probability.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use gradual onset alone to exclude dissection in patients with other high-risk features (Marfan/aortic disease, pulse deficit, neurologic deficit, new murmur, hypotension).
ask.escalation_warning: Abrupt severe chest/back pain with hypotension, pulse deficit, or neurologic deficit is a dissection or ruptured AAA until proven otherwise: immediate CT angiography and surgical notification.

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
evidence.population: Consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection from 21 studies (case series; sensitivity pooled; LR- derived from comparison cohorts)
evidence.quote: sudden onset (sensitivity, 84%). The absence of sudden pain onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (negative likelihood ratio [LR], 0.3; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.2-0.5)
evidence.reference_standard: Dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery, or autopsy
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (finding: sudden-onset pain)

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Um J, Anjum O, et al. High risk clinical features for acute aortic dissection: a case-control study. Acad Emerg Med. 2018;25(4):378-384.
evidence.population: Matched case-control: 194 ED/in-hospital CT- or echo-confirmed AAD cases vs 776 ED controls with truncal pain <14 days and no clear diagnosis
evidence.quote: Absence of abrupt-onset pain (sensitivity = 95.9%, negative likelihood ratio = 0.07 [0.03-0.14]) can help rule out AAD.
evidence.reference_standard: CT angiography or echocardiography confirmed dissection
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection (finding: abrupt-onset pain)

ask.how: Ask an open question about how the pain began, then specifically: 'Did it reach its worst within seconds, or build up over minutes?' Document time-to-peak intensity and whether the patient can pinpoint the moment of onset (what they were doing). Also ask about tearing/ripping quality and migration.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of sudden onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (LR- 0.3 in the RCE pooled series; 0.07 in an ED case-control study), but the clinical examination is insufficiently sensitive to rule out dissection on its own.
ask.pitfalls: Patients recall onset imprecisely, particularly after analgesia or when pain was preceded by exertion; gradual-onset presentations still occur in ~5-16% of dissections, especially in elderly patients or with painless neurologic presentations.
ask.positive_finding: Abrupt-onset pain is present in ~84-96% of aortic dissections but is common in other conditions, so it raises suspicion for dissection only modestly (specificity not established in unselected cohorts); it is a high-risk feature in the ADD risk score.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give history; otherwise ask witnesses or EMS about onset.
ask.title: Pain abrupt in onset and maximal at onset (thunderclap-type chest/back pain)

ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

evidence.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis (imaging-confirmed)

evidence.population: Consecutive unselected outpatients with suspected DVT, 14 studies (>8000 patients)
evidence.quote: prevalence of DVT in the low, moderate, and high clinical probability groups was 5.0% (95% CI, 4.0%-8.0%), 17% (95% CI, 13%-23%), and 53%
evidence.reference_standard: Imaging plus 3-month clinical follow-up
evidence.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis, prevalence by Wells clinical probability category

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

examine.changes_what: SBP <90/MAP <65: resuscitate, lactate, POCUS (RUSH) to classify shock type, cause-directed therapy now. Normal BP: keep looking for compensated shock (HR, lactate, mentation, urine output).
examine.contraindications: Avoid the arm with a dialysis fistula, lymphoedema or recent axillary surgery; none otherwise.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a single normal cuff reading to exclude shock or tamponade; do not interpret SBP <90 as 'baseline' without documented prior values.
examine.escalation_warning: SBP <90 or MAP <65 with altered mentation, lactate >2, oliguria or cool skin is shock: immediate resuscitation and senior/ICU review; in suspected dissection or tamponade, hypotension signals imminent collapse.

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Kareemi HK, Wells G, Perry JJ. Clinical examination for acute aortic dissection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2019.
evidence.population: Pooled 4 studies of ED patients evaluated for suspected acute aortic dissection (review total 9 studies, 2,400 participants; prevalence range 21.9-76.1%)
evidence.quote: hypotension (n = 4, specificity = 95%, LR+ = 2.9 95% CI = 1.8-4.6, I2 = 42%)
evidence.reference_standard: Acute aortic dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery or autopsy per primary studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection; finding = hypotension as defined by each primary study (thresholds varied; not uniformly SBP <90 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Drazner MH, Hellkamp AS, Leier CV, Shah MR, Miller LW, Russell SD, Young JB, Califf RM, et al. Value of clinician assessment of hemodynamics in advanced heart failure: the ESCAPE trial. Circ Heart Fail. 2009.
evidence.location: Table 5 (Utility of history and physical examination in detecting an invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2); columns frequency, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, LR+, LR-, OR, P
evidence.population: 188 patients hospitalised with advanced decompensated HF in the ESCAPE trial with pulmonary artery catheter measurements
evidence.reference_standard: Invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 by pulmonary artery catheter
evidence.target_condition: Low cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 in advanced heart failure; finding = SBP <90 mmHg on baseline examination

evidence.citation: Guberman BA, Fowler NO, Engel PJ, Gueron M, Allen JM. Cardiac tamponade in medical patients. Circulation. 1981.
evidence.population: 56 medical patients with cardiac tamponade, single-centre case series, University of Cincinnati
evidence.quote: heart sounds were diminished in 19 patients; arterial systolic pressure was greater than or equal to 100 mm Hg in 35
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/haemodynamic diagnosis of tamponade with relief by pericardiocentesis or pericardial resection
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade (sensitivity only); finding = systolic BP <100 mmHg (threshold differs from id title's <90)

examine.how: Measure with a correctly sized cuff on a supported arm (manual if the automated reading is doubtful or the pulse is irregular), repeat, and measure both arms when dissection is possible; calculate MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP)/3. Interpret against the patient's usual pressure and drug list.
examine.negative_finding: A normal SBP does not exclude shock (compensated haemorrhage, early sepsis, cardiogenic shock with vasoconstriction) or tamponade (about 60% of tamponade patients had SBP ≥100), nor low cardiac index in heart failure (SBP <90 sensitivity 12%).
examine.pitfalls: Chronic hypertensives are hypoperfused at 'normal' pressures; beta-blockers, pacemakers and automated cuffs in AF mislead. Interarm difference >20 mmHg raises dissection concern. Cuff readings overestimate true pressure in profound vasoconstriction.
examine.positive_finding: SBP <90 (or MAP <65) is shock until proven otherwise and should trigger a search for the cause (septic, hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic, cardiogenic, obstructive: tamponade/PE/tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, adrenal). In suspected dissection, hypotension roughly triples the odds (LR+ 2.9, specificity 95%). It is not a discriminator between causes.
examine.prerequisites: Appropriate cuff size; awareness of baseline BP, beta-blockers/antihypertensives and pacing.
examine.title: Systolic BP <90 mmHg (or MAP <65) at the bedside

examine.changes_what: Elevated JVP moves dyspnea/edema toward acute HF or RV/pericardial disease and away from hypovolemia; a flat JVP in hypotension favors hypovolemia/sepsis over cardiogenic causes.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm neck pressure in patients with carotid disease.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal JVP to withhold treatment for suspected heart failure, or declare a shocked patient hypovolemic when the neck cannot be adequately examined (obesity, short neck, column above the jaw).
examine.escalation_warning: Elevated JVP with hypotension, clear lungs and tachycardia suggests tamponade, RV infarction or massive PE and needs immediate echo/POCUS rather than diuresis.

evidence.citation: Butman SM, Ewy GA, Standen JR, Kern KB, Hahn E. Bedside cardiovascular examination in patients with severe chronic heart failure: importance of rest or inducible jugular venous distension. J Am Coll Cardiol 1993;22(4):968-74.
evidence.population: 52 patients with severe chronic heart failure undergoing in-hospital transplant evaluation; index finding = jugular venous distension at rest OR inducible by the abdominojugular test
evidence.quote: had the best combination of sensitivity (81%), specificity (80%) and predictive accuracy (81%) for elevation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
evidence.reference_standard: Right heart catheterization (PCWP >= 18 mmHg)
evidence.target_condition: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (>=18 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Signs and symptoms in adult patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med 2018;25(1):3-11 (author list not retrievable via abstract tool; confirmed by PMID/DOI).
evidence.population: Adults with a new episode of acute dyspnea; 8 ED studies, 4737 patients; HF prevalence 25-59%
evidence.quote: Elevated jugular venous pressure (0.88, pooled odds ratio: 7), added third heart sound (0.97), and lung crepitations (0.77, pooled odds ratio: 11)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of HF per included studies (varied)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnea

evidence.citation: Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess 2009;13(32):1-207.
evidence.population: Patients with suspected heart failure in primary care; individual patient data meta-analysis of 9 studies
evidence.quote: orthopnoea (89%), oedema (72%), elevated jugular venous pressure (70%), cardiomegaly (85%), added heart sounds (99%), lung crepitations (81%)
evidence.reference_standard: Echocardiography / expert panel per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (new diagnosis) in primary care

examine.how: Recline the patient at 30-45 degrees (adjust until the top of the pulsation is visible), turn the head slightly left, and use tangential light to find the top of the internal jugular column. Measure its vertical height above the sternal angle; >3 cm above the angle (about >8 cm H2O total) is elevated.
examine.negative_finding: A flat or normal JVP lowers but does not exclude heart failure; sensitivity is modest (roughly 0.2-0.7 across ED studies) and pooled sensitivity in ED series stays below 0.55.
examine.pitfalls: Confusing carotid with venous pulsation, misjudging the sternal angle-to-atrium distance (varies with position), and failing to see a very high column (look for earlobe pulsation) or a very low one (lie the patient flatter). Isolated RV failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade or constriction raise JVP without left-sided congestion.
examine.positive_finding: A venous column >3 cm above the sternal angle indicates raised right atrial pressure and, in chronic heart failure, usually raised left-sided filling pressure (PCWP >=18 mmHg). It substantially raises the probability of heart failure as the cause of acute dyspnea.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate light, exposed neck, patient relaxed and breathing quietly; identify the venous (biphasic, non-palpable, falls with inspiration, occludable) rather than carotid pulsation.
examine.title: Jugular venous pressure elevated (>8 cm H2O / >3 cm above sternal angle); low/flat JVP as the negative

examine.changes_what: Positive in inferior MI: obtain right-sided ECG leads/echo and avoid preload reduction (nitrates, diuretics); positive with oedema/ascites: pursue constriction or RV failure by echo.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use to diagnose or exclude tamponade, and do not rely on it when the JVP cannot be seen.
examine.escalation_warning: Kussmaul sign with hypotension and clear lungs in inferior MI = RV infarction: give fluids cautiously, avoid nitrates/diuretics, and expedite reperfusion; with muffled sounds and pulsus paradoxus consider effusive-constrictive disease and urgent echo.

evidence.citation: Dube E, Crozier M, Middleton A, Best B, Ohle R. Kussmaul's sign for the diagnosis of right ventricular myocardial infarction: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies. CJEM. 2021.
evidence.population: 469 consecutive patients with acute inferior MI, pooled from 8 diagnostic-accuracy studies (1965-2019 literature)
evidence.quote: Kussmaul's sign had a sensitivity of 62.5% (44.6, 77.5), specificity 90% (73.0, 96.8), negative likelihood ratio (LR) 0.2 (0.1-0.8) and positive LR 5.8 (2.5, 13.3)
evidence.reference_standard: Combined reference standards across studies (echocardiography, haemodynamics, ECG/angiography as defined per study)
evidence.target_condition: Right ventricular myocardial infarction in patients admitted with acute inferior myocardial infarction

examine.how: Position the patient so the top of the jugular venous column is visible (usually 30-45 degrees), identify the JVP and its meniscus, then ask for a slow deep inspiration through the mouth. Normally the column falls; Kussmaul sign is present when it fails to fall or rises with inspiration.
examine.negative_finding: Absence lowers the probability of RV infarction in inferior MI (LR- about 0.2) but does not exclude constriction or RV failure; it says little about tamponade, where the sign is usually absent anyway.
examine.pitfalls: Requires a visible JVP - obesity, a very high JVP above the mandible, or shallow breathing hide it. Kussmaul sign with pulsus paradoxus suggests effusive-constrictive disease rather than simple tamponade.
examine.positive_finding: A positive sign indicates impaired right-heart filling with inspiration - RV infarction in the setting of inferior MI (LR+ about 6), constrictive pericarditis, severe RV failure/pulmonary hypertension, or massive PE; it is classically absent in pure tamponade.
examine.prerequisites: Visible JVP (exclude hepatojugular pressure); patient able to breathe deeply on command.
examine.title: Kussmaul sign: JVP rises (or fails to fall) with inspiration

examine.changes_what: Prolonged CRT in shock: treat as ongoing hypoperfusion and reassess after resuscitation; normal CRT does not rule out hypovolemia.
examine.contraindications: Not interpretable on a cold, cyanotic or vasoconstricted limb, with peripheral arterial disease, or in the presence of nail polish/false nails.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use CRT to exclude hypovolemia or bleeding in adults; do not interpret on cold, vasoconstricted or peripherally diseased limbs.
examine.escalation_warning: Persistently prolonged CRT after initial resuscitation in septic shock marks a high-mortality group and should prompt reassessment of perfusion and escalation, not reassurance.

evidence.citation: Schriger DL, Baraff LJ. Capillary refill--is it a useful predictor of hypovolemic states? Ann Emerg Med. 1991;20(6):601-605.
evidence.population: 13 adult ED patients with history suggestive of hypovolemia and hypotension; comparison group blood donors
evidence.quote: 26% for the orthostatic group, and 46% for the hypotensive group
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical hypovolemia group assignment (hypotension); age-sex specific CRT upper limit of normal
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolemia (ED patients with suggestive history and frank hypotension)

evidence.citation: Schriger DL, Baraff LJ. Capillary refill--is it a useful predictor of hypovolemic states? Ann Emerg Med. 1991;20(6):601-605.

evidence.citation: Jacquet-Lagreze M, Wiart C, Schweizer R, et al. Prognostic value of capillary refill time in adult patients: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Crit Care. 2023;27(1):473.
evidence.population: Adults with acute circulatory failure; 13 studies in primary analysis (23 studies, 60,656 patients overall)
evidence.quote: pooled sensitivity was 54% (95%CI [43; 64]). The pooled specificity was 72% (95%CI [55; 84])
evidence.reference_standard: Mortality as reported by each study
evidence.target_condition: Death in adults with acute circulatory failure (abnormal CRT, study-specific thresholds)

examine.how: With the hand at heart level in a warm room, press the distal index finger pad (or nail bed) firmly for 10-15 s until blanched, release, and time return of baseline colour with a watch. Prolonged is >3 s (ICU studies use >2.4-3 s at the fingertip; knee CRT is an alternative site).
examine.negative_finding: A normal CRT does not exclude mild-to-moderate hypovolemia in adults (sensitivity 6% after 450 mL loss). In acute circulatory failure, normal CRT only weakly lowers mortality risk (pooled LR- about 0.6).
examine.pitfalls: Cold room, cold hands, age and vasoconstriction prolong CRT without hypoperfusion; measurement quality (site, pressure, timing) strongly affects accuracy. CRT is a prognostic/perfusion marker, not a diagnostic test for the cause of shock.
examine.positive_finding: In resuscitated septic shock, a fingertip CRT >2.4 s at 6 h predicts 14-day death with sensitivity 82% and specificity 73%, and marks persisting hypoperfusion. In undifferentiated adults, a prolonged CRT is a weak sign of hypovolemia (sensitivity 26-46%).
examine.prerequisites: Warm extremity and ambient temperature; a second hand or watch to time; consistent pressure (a glass slide can standardise blanching).
examine.title: Capillary refill time prolonged (>2-3 s, fingertip at heart level, warm room)
